Simón Bolívar. The Venezuelan military leader and statesman who liberated six nations from Spanish colonial rule through a series of successful military campaigns across South America. Known as El Libertador, he envisioned a unified continent but ultimately failed to establish lasting political unity despite his military victories.

Bolívar led the independence movements of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, which is named after him, and Panama. He won decisive victories at the Battle of Boyacá in 1819 and the Battle of Carabobo in 1821, turning the tide against Spanish forces. Having established the independence of these territories, Bolívar declared himself dictator of Gran Colombia and attempted to establish a continental federation of newly independent nations. He founded Bolivia in 1825 and presided over the drafting of its constitution. But internal conflicts and political fragmentation left him disillusioned. In 1830, he resigned from power and died in exile in Colombia. His vision of a unified South American state proved unrealistic. Gran Colombia dissolved shortly after his departure, fragmenting into the separate nations we know today.
